angle: This deck is famous for a four-card storm kill and wins with a two-card invoice: the Aetherflux Reservoir ledger assembles in 0.7% of games while the donation engine and a punisher come together in 56.7%, so the issue teaches you to fly the deck you actually have and to recognise the one game in a hundred and fifty where the other one shows up.

teases: The fifteen-cast Reservoir ledger, walked in full — and measured at 0.7% of games
Hullbreaker Horror plus Sol Ring: the database says infinite, the rules say no
Ten cards fill three hands. Six cards send the bill.
Blue pays 79.2% of the pips off 63.4% of the sources

departments.note: Full-bleed commander art. The issue.json tagline 'Everyone draws. Everyone pays.' is the thesis in four words, and the kicker is the whole issue: the deck's median engine against its famous one. Both violators are literally true — six checker-passed case files, two of which are refutations (001, 005), and a 10,000-iteration goldfish at seed 42.
Renderer-standard Flight Plan: five acts, promises verbatim from issue_spec, tier legend and masthead trio printed in full.

departments.headline: ONE PIP, FORTY BLUE CARDS
departments.dek: Why is a mono-white god running a blue deck? Read the activation cost. Colour identity counts every mana symbol printed on a card, rules text included — and one Phyrexian pip in the fine print pays for the whole blue half of this 99.
departments.body:
Exhibit one. Heliod, the Radiant Dawn is a white card: {2}{W}{W}, a 4/4 God whose entry returns an enchantment from your graveyard. His colour identity is blue and white anyway. CR 903.4 counts every mana symbol anywhere on the card, and the transform ability reads {3}{U/P}. One hybrid Phyrexian pip in an activation cost is why forty cards in this deck are allowed to ask for blue mana.

Now the guarantee, which is the reason the 99 looks like this. Your commander begins the game in the command zone and is the only card you always have (CR 903.4). Every table-draw engine here was chosen because the back face converts opponents' draws into your discount and your flash. The goldfish casts him on a median turn 4 and has him available in 90.2% of games by turn six.

The tax is on the record: {2}{W}{W} the first time, and each recast from the zone costs {2} more than the last (CR 903.8). Four mana, then six, then eight. Heliod also owes a toll nobody prints — every trip home refunds the flip, so you pay {3}{U/P} again, at sorcery speed only, on a later turn.

Coach's ledger on that: insure, do not re-buy. The Phyrexian pip takes two life instead of blue mana, Teferi's Protection buys a whole turn of immunity, and a held Swan Song is cheaper than paying both tolls twice. In this deck protection is the better spend by a wide margin.

Is the 21-damage clock a plan here (CR 903.10a)? No — a coincidence. The back face is a 4/6 that would need six clean connections in a deck whose attack step is ceremonial. Your clocks are Iron Maiden, Ebony Owl Netsuke and a Reservoir ledger.

The political read is worth more than the combat math. The front face registers as a harmless enchantment rebuy, and the flip is your tell: the turn the Warped Eclipse shows up, three opponents learn you have instant-speed range and a discount that grows every time they draw. Spend that information on the turn you choose.

captions.Heliod, the Radiant Dawn // Heliod, the: **THE TELL:** the front face is camouflage; the flip announces instant-speed range and a discount that scales with the table's own draws. Pay the {U/P} with two life whenever the blue mana is doing counter duty.

pilot_tips.card: Heliod, the Radiant Dawn // Heliod, the Warped Eclipse
pilot_tips.text: Transform only at sorcery speed, so plan the flip a full rotation ahead and pay the Phyrexian pip with life whenever your blue mana is holding up a counterspell.

departments.pull_quote: A god's colour identity turns on the fine print. One Phyrexian pip, forty blue cards.

departments.headline: PUNISHER FIRST, GIFTS SECOND
departments.dek: Why would a control deck hand three opponents free cards every turn? Because ten cards in this 99 fill their hands and six cards charge for the result — and both halves are on the battlefield in 56.7% of games. The order is the whole skill.

captions.Iron Maiden: **THE INVOICE:** hand size minus 4, to each opponent, on each opponent's own upkeep — before they get to spend a single card you gave them.
captions.Howling Mine: **THE TAP:** two mana, one extra card a head, every draw step. Cheap, quiet, and a straight donation until something is billing for it.
captions.Forced Fruition: **THE FIREHOSE:** seven cards per opposing spell. Stack 003 confirms the cards arrive even if the enchantment dies in response — so land it when the meter can convert it.

pilot_tips.text: Lead with Scrawling Crawler whenever it is in your opener — it hands out the cards and bills for them in the same permanent, which is the only card here that lets you skip the wait.

departments.pull_quote: A Howling Mine with nothing behind it is you paying three opponents rent.

departments.headline: SORTED BY WHO PAYS
departments.dek: Sixty-six spells, 33 lands, Heliod in the command zone — and the order on this page is the order that wins games. The six cards that charge lead. The ten that hand out cards follow. The kill sits exactly where its 0.7% says it belongs.

roster.role: The burst and the value layer
The base that makes either colour

captions.Iron Maiden: **THE LOAD-BEARING CARD:** three mana for a clock that bills three players, computed on resolution and paid on their upkeep. Everything in the firehose exists to feed it.
captions.Hullbreaker Horror: **THE SINGLE POINT:** the kill's only creature, and Enlightened Tutor cannot reach it. Long-Term Plans is the one card in this 99 that can go and find him.
captions.Thought Vessel: **THE SLEEPER:** stack 004's loop accepts any two-mana rock, so this one moonlights as a kill piece while wearing a utility card's face — and it deletes your own maximum hand size on the way.

pilot_tips.text: Land Folio of Fancies before a big draw turn — nobody discards down to seven any more, so Iron Maiden's hand-size-minus-4 loses its ceiling.

departments.note: Basics, the utility lands, the rocks and the two medallions fall to the automatic Depth group deliberately — depth should read as depth, and here the depth is the mana.

departments.headline: TWO LANDS, A TAP, AND A NO
departments.dek: What separates the 73.8% of first sevens you keep from the quarter you ship? Not power — pairing. Two to five lands, something that fills hands, something that empties them. Four real hands below. Call each one out loud before you read the verdict.

hands.why: Three lands, a rock, a tax, a no, and a tap. Ancient Tomb into a two-mana rock beats the median Heliod turn of 4 outright, and the Mine simply waits in hand until something is charging for it. This is the shape you are actually looking for.

Three punishers and nothing to wind them. Nobody's hand reaches seven cards on its own, and the pair you need assembles by turn six in only 41.2% of games — this hand contributes nothing to that number. Two punishers and no engine is a mulligan every time, however clean the mana looks.

Both reliable axes at once. A table-draw engine turns up by turn six in 75.4% of games and free or cheap interaction in 67.2%, and this hand opens with one of each on turn two. Dig Through Time is the payoff the Remora fills for you.

Ledger's confession: the simulator keeps every hand with two to five lands, so it keeps this one and inflates its own 73.8%. You are smarter than the simulator. Five lands, two seven-drops, and nothing to do before turn five — the base is fine, this flood is the hand's fault.

pilot_tips.text: Keep almost any hand pairing Ancient Tomb with a two-mana rock — that exact pair is this deck's turn-three commander, and two life is the cheapest acceleration you will be offered.

departments.pull_quote: Two punishers and no engine is a mulligan wearing a game plan.

departments.headline: TWO TURNS THAT DECIDE IT
departments.dek: Turn six, Forced Fruition in your hand, a spellslinger two seats over. Then a quiet turn with the flip and your counter mana on the same scales. Commit out loud before you read our call.
departments.note: No furniture here on purpose. Decision 001 resolves to the punisher-first line and 002 to the early flip, so no tip, caption or callout may name Netsuke deployment or flip timing — the branches have to carry themselves or the spread stops being a question.

departments.headline: FIFTEEN CASTS, THREE FUNERALS
departments.dek: Six lines went to the desk and six came back cleared — two of them cleared as denials, which are the best reading in the issue. Start with the seven damage that lands on somebody else's upkeep. Finish with the ledger that pays fifty life three times and keeps the change.

callouts.title: THE LINE THAT PAYS RENT
callouts.text: Stack 003, and the one you will actually cast. Forced Fruition's trigger goes on the stack above the spell that caused it, so destroying the enchantment afterwards claws nothing back (113.7a). Ebony Owl Netsuke's intervening 'if' checks seven cards at trigger and again at resolution; Iron Maiden carries no such clause and computes hand size minus 4 on resolution. Holding: 4 plus 3 against a seven-card hand — 7 damage in one upkeep, 18 down to 11, and you spent no mana on their turn.

callouts.title: OPEN THE LOOP
callouts.text: Stack 004. Cast Arcane Signet; Hullbreaker Horror's trigger targets Sol Ring, which is a permanent and therefore a legal target, and each cast bounces the other rock. Three mana spent, three mana produced, per full cycle. Exactly neutral, never positive — and unbounded in casts within one main phase.

callouts.title: RUN THE METER
callouts.text: Stack 006. Aetherflux Reservoir gains you 1 life for each spell cast this turn, so cast n banks n and k casts bank k(k+1)/2. Casts one through six take 32 life to 53. Pay 50, point it at the seat on 26, and they leave at −24 while you sit on 3.

callouts.title: TWICE MORE, EXACTLY
callouts.text: Casts seven through twelve rebuild you to 60; pay 50 at the seat on 40 and they die at −10. Casts thirteen through fifteen reach 52; pay 50 at the seat on 34 and they die at −16. You end on 2 life with the loop still available. Fifteen is the proven minimum: fourteen casts bank 105 against a requirement of 119.

callouts.title: THE WINDOWS NOBODY CLOSES
callouts.text: The same record, read the other way. Activating is not casting, so the Horror never triggers during an activation, and the loop's artifact casts are only legal with an empty stack — they cannot be made in response to anything. Every loop cast and every fifty-life payment hands priority to three awake opponents, and this engine defends none of it. Grand Abolisher is in the 99 and was not on that board; whether his static closes these particular windows is not something the record settles.

captions.Iron Maiden: **THE MEDIAN KILL:** stack 003's holding, in three mana. Seven damage in a single upkeep, paid before your opponent gets to spend the hand you filled.
captions.Aetherflux Reservoir: **THE CONVERTER:** cast n, gain n. That is why the ceiling is an arithmetic problem rather than a board problem — and why fourteen casts is not enough.
captions.Grand Abolisher: **THE MISSING SHIELD:** the record names the open windows and names this card as the thing built to close them. The walkthrough that proves it is the issue's most wanted case.

pilot_tips.text: Lead the commit turn with Grand Abolisher rather than deploying him a turn early — a shield left standing through a full rotation is an announcement, and three players answer announcements.

departments.pull_quote: Fifteen casts is the proven minimum. Fourteen banks 105 against a bill of 119.
departments.note: Case files render in numeric order with their intros from manual_prose.combo_lines. The furniture deliberately opens on 003 — the verified line the deck actually casts — so the ledger reads as the ceiling rather than the plan.

departments.headline: THE INVOICE GOES PUBLIC
departments.dek: When does the friendliest seat become the archenemy? Not the turn you cast the Reservoir. The turn Iron Maiden joins a Mine that is already running — and you want to know that turn before your three opponents do.

callouts.title: THE THREAT WINDOW
callouts.text: A punisher on the battlefield alongside any donation engine that is already running. The damage stops being a curiosity and becomes a clock, and every card you handed out turns into evidence. Forced Fruition resolving flips you instantly — seven cards per spell is a price the whole table starts paying at once.

callouts.title: SPEND THE GOODWILL FIRST
callouts.text: The early Mines and the Kwain taps are real gifts. Say so, let three players spend them, and bank the credit for the turn your upkeeps start collecting. Your library and your hand are invisible; the table only assesses what you cast, so a Font of Mythos held two turns costs you nothing.

callouts.title: DON'T CONFESS EARLY
callouts.text: Aetherflux Reservoir standing next to Hullbreaker Horror is a confession, and anyone who has done the reading solves it on sight. Deploy the Reservoir on the commit turn itself, never a turn early to develop — and use Enlightened Tutor as a scheduler, fired on the end step before your untap so your draw step delivers the piece.

captions.The Second Doctor: **THE POLITE NO:** every opponent who accepts a card can't attack you next turn. Generosity with a cover charge, and every answer they give you profits you.
captions.Propaganda: **THE TOLL BOOTH:** one enchantment blanks combat math from three seats at once. That is virtual card advantage, tripled.

pilot_tips.text: Never save Teferi's Protection as a combo shield — your life total can't change while it is up, so it can't share a turn with a ledger that pays fifty life three times. It is the card that buys back the turn you became the archenemy.

departments.pull_quote: The table forgives a Howling Mine. It never forgives an Iron Maiden with the Mine still running.

departments.headline: YOU ARE THE CONTROL SEAT
departments.dek: Which deck at this table actually kills you? Not the aggro player you sell attack taxes to. It is the combo pilot you just handed twenty-one cards — and against them you are the slower deck, so stop racing and start holding up mana.

threats.read: Assign yourself the control role and mean it. Your kill assembles in 0.7% of games, 2.4% with the tutor counted, at a mean turn of 6.809 — slower and rarer than a dedicated combo deck in this bracket, so you are never the racer here. What you are is well armed: free or cheap interaction is in hand in 78.1% of games and 67.2% by turn six. Spend it only on the card that ends the game. Forced Fruition stays in your hand against this seat — seven cards per spell is their dream turn — and Drannith Magistrate lands early to blank command-zone and cast-from-exile lines before they start.

Here is the good news nobody expects from a control deck: your win condition does not tap. Iron Maiden, Ebony Owl Netsuke and Viseling charge on each opponent's upkeep with no mana from you, so under a lock you land a punisher and settle in rather than trying to break out. Do not try to race a lock with the Reservoir. Be more generous, not less — the back face cuts your costs by one for every card your opponents drew this turn, which is a rebate the tax player cannot charge you for. Then answer the piece that beats you rather than the first inconvenience.

Your best seat at any table. In a draw-go standoff your punishers advance while both of you pass, so somebody else has to be the beatdown. Four planeswalkers live through every Supreme Verdict including your own, and yours resolves straight through their permission. Teferi, Hero of Dominaria is the mirror's best card: the +1 draws and untaps two lands at the next end step, so the clock ticks while the counter mana stays open. The real exposure is one artifact-and-enchantment sweeper taking the firehose and the meter in a single card — deploy in layers and never show both halves to the same board.

Two attack taxes and a rider that eats a whole combat step blank attack plans from three seats for one card each, and the punishers turn defence into a clock. The trap is structural: an aggressive deck empties its hand and your Mines refill it, so land Iron Maiden or Ebony Owl Netsuke before the firehose goes on, never after. Then forget the Reservoir in this matchup entirely — the ledger starts from 32 life and pays fifty three times, and against a fast board that life is not going to be there.

captions.Forced Fruition: **THE ONE GIFT YOU CAN REGRET:** seven cards to the caster of every opposing spell. Against a storm pilot that is their turn, not yours — this is the card that stays in hand.

pilot_tips.text: Know Drannith Magistrate's limit before you tap out — it stops casting from anywhere but hand, so it blanks flashback, escape and commander recasts and does nothing at all to a reanimation spell.

departments.headline: DELIVERIES, NOT ARRIVALS
departments.dek: Three tutors, and not one of them puts a card in your hand. Top, top, and third from the top — so before you name a card, count how many cards you are about to draw. In this 99 that number is rarely one.

captions.Long-Term Plans: **THE SECRET WISH:** third from the top, no reveal, and the only search in the 99 that can find a creature. On a bare board that is three draw steps; under a Font of Mythos it is your very next one.

pilot_tips.text: Ring Temple Bell at instant speed to pull a Long-Term Plans delivery a full turn forward — but only with a punisher already down, or you are paying three opponents for your own convenience.

departments.headline: BLUE DOES 79% OF THE WORK
departments.dek: Blue pays 79.2% of this deck's pips and owns 63.4% of its sources. Does that gap cost you a turn? On curve blue lands 74.2% of the time off lands alone and 83.9% once the rocks tap — and exactly one card in the 99 feels the difference.

captions.Ancient Tomb: **THE ACCELERANT:** two colourless a turn, sold to you two life at a time. It is raw speed, not a patch — 33 lands plus six rocks is 39 mana sources against a 37 yardstick.
captions.Smothering Tithe: **THE DOUBLE AGENT:** a Treasure every time an opponent draws and declines to pay {2}, in a deck built to make opponents draw. The audit counts it as a mana source for both colours, which is exactly right.
captions.Irrigated Farmland: **FLOOD INSURANCE:** one of only two lands here that always enters tapped, and on the turn you have six lands and no seventh play it stops being a land. Cycle it for {2} and draw.

pilot_tips.text: Treat Archmage's Charm as a turn-four card cast off duals and a Signet, never a turn-three promise — it is the only triple pip in the deck, and it has no generic mana for Heliod's discount to eat.

departments.pull_quote: Thirty-three lands and six rocks make 39 mana sources: short on lands, on target for mana.

departments.headline: THE SMALLEST NUMBER WINS
departments.dek: Ten thousand games at seed 42, no opponents and no removal, every assumption printed. The figure worth the page is the tiny one: the pair that actually wins turns up in 56.7% of games, and the kill everybody talks about in 0.7%.

captions.Long-Term Plans: **WHY 0.7% IS 0.7%:** the kill needs three groups at once and two of them are single named cards, and this is the only search in the deck that reaches the creature. That is the whole explanation.

departments.pull_quote: 0.7% is not a flaw in the simulation. It is what an AND of three groups looks like when two of them are one card each.

departments.headline: WHAT WOULD MOVE A NUMBER
departments.dek: Ten cards worth knowing about, each priced against something this deck actually measured. Six close an axis the audit flagged, three widen a kill that currently rests on one creature, and one turns a hoarded hand into a turn you schedule.
departments.pull_quote: Six copies is 36% of an opening seven. Seven copies is 41%. One card, five points, one mana.
departments.note: The renderer draws the ten and their evidence bullets from considering.json. Four of the ten rest on unwalked rules questions — Mana Vault's ledger, Tidespout Tyrant's mandatory target, and the Teferi loop — and the entries say so rather than pricing them as settled.

departments.headline: SIX CLEARED, TWO DENIED
departments.dek: Every step, every citation verbatim, nothing summarised. Read the denials first — the famous two-card infinite and the Kitten's mana claim are the best argument that everything else in this issue is true.

departments.headline: SEVENTY-FOUR HANDS
departments.dek: Nobody owns this deck's look. Eighty-five cards, 74 painters, and 66 of those cards are the only one their artist made for this list. Counted per card and never per copy — fourteen Islands count once, and that honesty is the whole point.

featured.note:
Three cards. That is the largest hand anyone holds in this deck, and three different painters hold it at once — Richard Wright, Kieran Yanner and Piotr Dura are tied at the top of a roster of 74.

We lead with Wright because his three sit on both halves of the plan. Alhammarret's Archive is the asymmetry argument in a single card: your draws double and your life gain doubles, and nobody else's does either. Skyscribing is the gift itself, X cards for every player at once. Mana Confluence is the land that charges you a life for the privilege of casting either colour.

Then the honest part, said plainly: this is not curation and we are not going to dress it up as taste. Eighty-five cards, 74 artists, and 66 of them appear exactly once. A list assembled one printing at a time out of thirty years of Magic looks precisely like this, and the breadth is the better story anyway — your kill piece, your counterspell and your shorelines each came from a different hand.

also_worth_noting.note: Tied at three, and his trio shares nothing but a brush: Drannith Magistrate, Metallurgic Summonings and Teferi's Ageless Insight. A hate bear, a token engine, and the second of the deck's two draw doublers.
The third artist at three, and the gentlest palette draws the plainest duty: Adarkar Wastes, Temple of Enlightenment and Swords to Plowshares. Two lands and the cheapest answer in the game.
The matched set. Pearl Medallion and Sapphire Medallion, one painter, one pair of cost-cutters — the only place in this deck where two cards obviously belong beside each other on the table.
The two biggest blue bodies in the 99, from the same hand: Hullbreaker Horror, who the whole ceiling runs through, and Torrential Gearhulk, who flashes in and recasts a counterspell for free.
Braingeyser and Temple Bell — two of the oldest ways this deck has of filling a hand, and both of them still doing the job.

departments.pull_quote: Three cards is the largest hand here. That is not taste — it is thirty years of printings, one card at a time.

departments.note: next_issue reads 'TO BE ANNOUNCED' in issue.json, so the teaser runs thin until a deck is named. Colophon carries the rules version and the decklist hash as standard.

rhythm_notes: Act I front-loads identity at medium-then-high intensity: the Command Zone teaches, the Game Plan states the thesis, and the 99 drops to browsing before Act II asks the reader to do anything. Act II climbs practice to participation to the peak — The Kill closes the act as the payoff to meeting the deck and learning to fly it, and it reads as narrative because five callout-steps walk the arithmetic as a story rather than a citation dump. Act III is three consecutive Coach sections and stays at medium: reflection, then reference, then instruction, so no two dense spreads touch. Act IV is the only genuinely dense run, and the declared full-bleed art break sits between Sources Say and By the Numbers exactly where the rhythm needs it; The Short List then drops to imagination before the opt-in depth of Judge's Desk, which is buffered on the far side by Featured Artist. What's Your Play? carries no furniture at all, deliberately — a tip or a caption there would telegraph a recommendation the reader is supposed to make first. Pun budget spent, all in furniture: 'The law office', 'The toll booth', 'Deliveries, not arrivals', 'Flood insurance'. Four.
gaps: No case file covers Grand Abolisher closing stack 006's priority windows. It is the deck's central protection rule and currently rests on oracle reading — and it has a genuine edge, since a channel ability is activated from a card in hand and Otawara, Soaring City is in this very manabase as proof the shape exists. Highest-value next stack by a distance.

Alhammarret's Archive doubling the Reservoir's life-gain trigger is unwalked. If it holds, it lowers the fifteen-cast minimum and the number of open windows the kill has to survive, and The Kill could cite a shorter ledger.

Stack 003 walked the punisher upkeep with the cleanup trim intact, but The Second Doctor and Folio of Fancies both delete maximum hand size. What Iron Maiden's uncapped X actually looks like across turns is unverified, and it is the deck's own headline interaction.

Four Short List entries turn on unwalked rules questions — Mana Vault's ledger against the exactly-neutral pair, Tidespout Tyrant's mandatory target, and the Teferi plus Displacer Kitten loop. Alms Collector sits off the list on a rules question rather than a deckbuilding one.

Strategy DB holes the frame names and this issue felt: nothing on the forced-draw punisher archetype as its own school, nothing on rating a win line by measured assembly rate rather than by power, nothing on priority-window management for a loop that opens a window every iteration, and nothing on hand-size taxation as a damage source.
issue.json next_issue is 'TO BE ANNOUNCED', so the Back Page closes the loop weakly until the next volume is named.
